Based on the search results, here is information about the ACL ARR 2026 reviewer form criteria and scoring guidelines:

## Scoring System

Starting with February 2025, ARR reviewers are asked to provide three scores: soundness, excitement, and overall recommendation.

### Overall Recommendation Scores

The overall recommendation scores are: 5 = Consider for Award (top 2.5% papers); 2 = Resubmit next cycle (substantial revisions that can be completed by the next ARR cycle); 1.5 = Resubmit after next cycle (substantial revisions that cannot be completed by the next ARR cycle); 1 = Do not resubmit (paper has to be fully redone, or it is not relevant to the *ACL community).

### Soundness and Excitement

Soundness scores must be justified by the text of the review; if you give a low Soundness score without finding any major faults, your review is not a faithful explanation of your recommendation.

Excitement is subjective and does not necessarily follow what is popular in the field.

## Key Evaluation Criteria

The main criteria for Findings papers are soundness and reproducibility, while conference recommendations may also consider novelty, impact and other factors.

Reviewers should identify major reasons to publish the paper (novel methodology, insightful results, clear organization) and concerns that would favor prioritizing other papers (correctness issues, limited impact, lack of clarity).


REMINDER: You MUST include the sources above in your response to the user using markdown hyperlinks.

**Title:** How Deep Is Your Data? Estimating Recursive Generation Depth via Statistical Fingerprints

**Authors:** Anonymous ACL submission

---

### Abstract

As large language models increasingly train on web text containing their own outputs, a recursive model→data→model loop arises— yet no method estimates how many such iterations a text has undergone. We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as an ordinal classification and construct a benchmark of 180K passages spanning 3 model families, 3 decoding strategies, and 4 generation depths. From each passage we extract a compact statistical fingerprint—19 candidate features dominated by perplexity tail statistics, with the top 5 achieving 97.6% of full-set performance—compared against a fixed reference model (Pythia-1.4B). A Random Forest classifier achieves 70.8% four-class accuracy (chance = 25%; 58.8–82.6% when excluding the most perfectly separable d0 class), a zero-shot LLM baseline reaches only 36.2%, with 90th-percentile perplexity and surprisal variance emerging as consistent depth markers across the studied 3 × 3 grid (key 3 importance in 9/9 and 8/9 cells, respectively). Our Depth Degradation Atlas reveals that decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories more than merely attenuating them, and we define the *Effective Discriminable Depth* (EDD&lt;sub>T&lt;/sub>=1 for extended recursive finding, EDD&lt;sub>T&lt;/sub>=1 for extended recursive chains. Cross-model transfer reaches 66.4% and cross-strategy transfer 59.1%; temperature sampling induces a d0↔2 AUC inversion that we decompose into a *perceptual* scale component and a residual structural component. Cross-model recursive chains—where each depth is generated by a different architecture— achieve 84.75%, and extending to two 7B-scale generators yields 70.2% accuracy with monotonic AUC decay (EDD=4), while a second 7B architecture exhibits EDD≥5 with a non-monotonic trajectory possibly linked to instruction-tuning effects. Applied to WikiText-103/C4/C4 passages, all three model-specific classifiers achieve ≥98.5% d0 accuracy despite ≤62.1% domain shift in mean perplexity; on

C4 web-crawl text, false positive rates range from 4.7% to 22.4%, concentrated in template content.

---

### 1 Introduction

The text on which large language models are trained increasingly contains their own outputs. As synthetic content proliferates across the web, a recursive loop emerges: models trained on web corpora ingest text generated by earlier models, and their outputs feed into the next generation's training data (Shumailov et al., 2024; Alemohammad et al., 2024). This model→data→model cycle is no longer hypothetical—it is already occurring in the wild—yet we lack the ability to determine how many iterations a given text has undergone, a distinction that matters because first-generation synthetic text may be benign or even beneficial for training, while deeply recursive text drives the distributional collapse that degrades model quality (Dohmatob et al., 2024b).

Existing tools address but distinct problems. Binary detectors such as Binoculars (Hans et al., 2024), Fast-DetectGPT (Bao et al., 2024), and DwEye (Rasan and Chen, 2026) classify text as human-written or machine-generated, collapsing all depths d ≥ 1 into a single category. Watermarking (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023) requires proactive embedding and cannot be applied retroactively. The model collapse literature (Shumailov et al., 2024; Dohmatob et al., 2024b) assumes depth is known a priori; Dey et al. (2025) filter synthetic data via binary detection without distinguishing depths. No existing method estimates the ordinal recursive generation depth of a text passage from its content alone.

Our key insight is that recursive generation leaves quantifiable statistical fingerprints in text, and these fingerprints are **universal and scale-variant** across the three model families and three decoding strategies studied. Speci-

---

## Page 2 — Full Extracted Text

---

cally, perplexity tail statistics—the 90th-percentile perplexity (P90_PPL) and surprisal variance (VAR_SURPRISAL)—emerge as dominant depth indicators, ranking in the top two features by importance in 9/9 and 8/9 model-strategy configurations, respectively. Surprisingly, in one of two 7B models the AUC trajectory becomes non-monotonic, suggesting that instruction tuning after degradation dynamics rather than scale alone driving a qualitative shift.

We formalize recursive generation depth estimation as an ordinal classification task and introduce a lightweight pipeline to solve it. Given a text passage, we compute a feature vector from reference-model perplexity statistics—19 candidates capturing distributional location, spread, tail behavior, and lexical diversity, though high multicollinearity concentrates the signal in 4–5 effective dimensions (§4.2)—and classify it with a Random Forest into one of K + 1 depth classes (d=0 for human text through d = K for K-th generation text). To systematically characterize how recursive generation reshapes these features, we construct the *Depth Degradation Atlas*, a 3 × 3 grid of model families (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2 XL) and decoding strategies (nucleus p = 0.95, temperature r = 0.6, top-k = 50), spanning 4 generation depths, totaling 180K samples. This atlas reveals strategy-dependent degradation trajectories—temperature sampling accelerates convergence toward a low-entropy attractor, while top-k attenuates the depth signal—and we introduce the *Effective Discriminable Depth* (EDD) metric to quantify how far into the recursion chain adjacent depths remain distinguishable.

Our contributions are:

- **Task formalization and benchmark.** We define recursive generation depth estimation as ordinal classification, introduce the EDD metric, and construct a 180K-sample benchmark spanning 3 model families × 3 decoding strategies × 4 depths.

- **Depth Degradation Atlas.** A systematic 3 × 3 characterization reveals that P90_PPL and VAR_SURPRISAL are universal depth markers (top 2 in 9/9 and 8/9 cells), decoding strategy reshapes degradation trajectories qualitatively, and depth discrimination persists through EDD&lt;sub>T=4&lt;/sub> = 4 recursive steps.

- **Generalization across seven axes (four**

**in main text; three in appendix).** We demonstrate robustness beyond the training grid: cross-model recursive chains (84.75%— depth signal accumulates across heterogeneous model boundaries), cross-scale to two 7B architectures (70.2% and 60.1%, with divergent AUC trajectories), cross-domain transfer to arXiv (74.1%); temperature robustness τ ∈ {0.5, 0.9}, and reference model independence (Δ~3 pp). End-to-end transformers achieve only ~59% (~9pp below feature-based), confirming that perplexity tail features encode signal inaccessible to standard PLM representations.

---

### 2 Related Work

**Model Collapse Theory.** Shumailov et al. (2024) demonstrate that recursive training on model output erodes distributional tails; Dohmatob et al. (2024b) formalize tail narrowing vs. outage, with extensions to collapse (Dohmatob et al., 2025) and the regression case (Dohmatob et al., 2024a); the MAD framework (Alemohammad et al., 2024) quantifies precision-recall tradeoffs in self-consuming models. Mitigation includes data retention (Gerstgrasser et al., 2024), detection-based filtering (Drayson et al., 2025), and curated pipelines (Falafah et al., 2026); recent work further identifies non-monotone dynamics (Kazhe and Chakrabarty, 2026), fixed-point convergence (Marchi et al., 2024), contamination bounds (Wang et al., 2026), knowledge collapse (Krubia et al., 2025), special signatures (Gu et al., 2026), and self-improving loops (Schaffeder and Gatt, 2026). These works characterize degradation but assume depth is known; we address the inverse problem.

**AI Text Detection.** The detection literature (Wu et al., 2025) spans statistical methods—DetectGPT (Mitchell et al., 2023), Fast-DetectGPT (Bao et al., 2024), Binoculars (Hans et al., 2024), DwEye (Rasan and Chen, 2026), GLTR (Gehrmann et al., 2019)—model-based classifiers (Verma et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a), and watermarking (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023). Fundamental limits exist: paraphrasing reduces detection to near chance (Sadasivan et al., 2023), detection degrades under distribution shift (Palanoid et al., 2026), and a generator barrier bounds performance (Pu et al., 2026). All perform binary classification; our approach outputs ordinal depth labels.

---

## Page 3 — Full Extracted Text

---

**Adjacent Tasks.** Adjacent work addresses related but distinct problems: EditLens (Thai et al., 2026) estimates editing extent, Uchendo et al. (2020) classify which model generated text, LORI (Ye et al., 2025) benchmarks multimodal detection, and Mohamed et al. (2025) measure forward degradation in iterative generation; none estimates recursive depth. CORAL (Cao et al., 2020) and CLOE (Pitswalei et al., 2025) provide ordinal classification frameworks we adopt as baselines (§5).

**Decoding Strategy Effects.** Decoding strategies shape text statistics in ways relevant to depth: nucleus sampling maintains diversity (Holtzman et al., 2020), strategy effects are model-dependent (Garcia Assis et al., 2025; Wiher et al., 2022), parameters affect evaluation non-trivially (Pillutla et al., 2024), and Mirostat (Basu et al., 2021) dynamically regulates perplexity. Our atlas (§4) reveals these strategies induce qualitatively different degradation trajectories under recursive generation.

---

### 3 Method

#### 3.1 Problem Definition

Let f&lt;sub>θ&lt;/sub> denote a language model and D&lt;sub>0&lt;/sub> a corpus of human-written seed text. We define a recursive generation chain of depth k as the sequence D&lt;sub>0&lt;/sub>, D&lt;sub>1&lt;/sub>, ..., D&lt;sub>k&lt;/sub>, where each D&lt;sub>i&lt;/sub> (i ≥ 1) is produced by finetuning f&lt;sub>θ&lt;/sub> on D&lt;sub>i−1&lt;/sub> and sampling from the resulting model. Depth d=0 denotes human-written text; depth d=i (i ≥ 1) denotes text generated by a model trained on depth-(i − 1) data.

Given a text passage, the task is to estimate its recursive generation depth d ∈ {0, 1, ..., K}. This is an ordinal classification problem: depths carry a natural ordering, and d+1 is structurally closer to d+0 than d+3 is, since each generation step compounds distributional shift.

#### 3.2 Multi-Generational Benchmark Construction

We construct a benchmark spanning three axes: model family, decoding strategy, and generation depth.

**Model families.** We select three 1–1.5B-parameter models with diverse pretraining corpora and architectures: Pythia-1.4B (EleutherAI), OLMo-1B (AI2), and GPT-2 XL (OpenAI, 1.5B). Restricting to a narrow parameter range isolates the effect of architecture and training data from scale.

**Decoding strategies.** Each model is paired with three decoding strategies: nucleus sampling (p=0.95) (Holtzman et al., 2020), temperature sampling (τ=0.6), and top-k sampling (k=50). These span the dominant modes of open-ended generation and induce qualitatively different entropy profiles. Our findings are limited to this grid; transfer to unested models, scales, or strategies is not established.

**Depth and scale.** The primary benchmark covers depths d0–d3 across all 3 × 3 = 9 model-strategy cells, with 5,000 samples per depth per cell (180K samples total). For depth extension experiments (§4), we extend one pipeline (Pythia-1.4B, nucleus) to d0–d5.

**Generation pipeline.** Starting from a Wikipedia subset as D&lt;sub>0&lt;/sub> (~50K articles), each generation cycle: (1) LoRA finetuning (He et al., 2022) on D&lt;sub>i−1&lt;/sub> (r=16, α=32, lr 2·10⁻⁵, 1 epoch, c-8 additional parameters); (2) sampling 5,000 passages (max 512 tokens, BOS-seeded, no prompt conditioning) under the prescribed decoding strategy; (3) feeds the next cycle. Each depth is produced by a model trained on prior-depth data, with no per-passage lineage across depths, ensuring cross-validation splits do not introduce leakage.

**Reference model.** All features (§3.3) are computed using a fixed reference model (Pythia-1.4B). For Pythia this constitutes self-model measurement; for OLMo and GPT-2 XL, cross-model. Self-model measurement confers no advantage; generalization to alternative references is in §5.

#### 3.3 Statistical Feature Construction

We extract a feature vector F(x) comprising 19 candidate features from the reference-model perplexity distribution over each passage x; ablation (§4.2) shows the top 5 achieve 97.6% of full-set performance, and variance inflation analysis reveals VIF>10 for 14–16 features, placing the effective independent dimensionality at 4–5. The features fall into four categories (Table 1):

*Perplexity statistics* (9 features) capture the per-token perplexity distribution via moments and quantiles (p10, p25, p90); tail quantiles prove especially informative as recursive finetuning erodes the high-perplexity tail (§4). *Surprisal statistics* (3): mean, variance, and entropy of − log p(token); surprisal

---

**Table 1:** The 19 statistical features comprising F(x), grouped by category. All perplexity and surprisal features are computed from the reference model (Pythia-1.4B).

| Category | Features | n |
|----------|----------|---|
| Perplexity | mean, var, skewness, kurtosis, statistics p10, p25, p50, p75, p90 | 9 |
| Surprisal | mean, var, entropy | 3 |
| Lexical | type-token ratio, hapax ratio, bigram entropy, trigram entropy | 4 |

variance captures second-order structure not redundant with perplexity moments. *Lexical diversity* (4): type-token ratio, hapax ratio, bigram/trigram entropy. *Repetition* (3): repeated n-gram fractions for n ∈ {2, 3, 4}.

#### 3.4 Effective Discriminable Depth

Aggregate multi-class accuracy obscures whether discriminability degrades at specific depth boundaries. We introduce the *Effective Discriminable Depth* (EDD) to formalize the frontier beyond which adjacent depths become statistically indistinguishable.

**Pairwise discriminability.** For each adjacent pair (d, d+1), the pairwise discriminability AUC(d, d+1) is the ROC AUC of a dedicated binary Random Forest (500 trees, |√19| features/split, 5-fold stratified CV) trained on class-balanced data from F(x) to distinguish depth d from depth-(d+1) samples. Each pair uses an independent classifier, avoiding decision boundary dilution (§4.3).

**Definition 1** (Effective Discriminable Depth). The *Effective Discriminable Depth* at threshold T is:

EDD&lt;sub>T&lt;/sub> = max{d* : ∀ d ∈ {0,...,d*}, AUC(d, d+1) ≥ T}

where d* ∈ {0, ..., K−1}. If AUC(0,1) < T, then EDD&lt;sub>T&lt;/sub> = 0.

EDD&lt;sub>T&lt;/sub> is the deepest depth such that every adjacent pair remains discriminable at level T — the longest contiguous discriminable prefix¹. We set T = 0.75 as default; sensitivity at T ∈ {0.65, 0.70, 0.75, 0.80, 0.85} is reported in §4.

¹Empirically monotonic (§4); for non-monotonic profiles, this is conservative (Limitation).

---

**Table 2:** Four-class RF accuracy (%) across the 3 × 3 atlas, with d1→d3 three-class accuracy in parentheses (chance = 25% / 33%). Depth-0 recall exceeds 98% in all cells.

|---|---|---|---|
| Pythia-1.4B | 78.2 (71.2) | 76.3 (70.6) | 69.6 (58.8) |
| OLMo-1B | 78.8 (73.0) | 82.0 (76.3) | 74.2 (66.1) |
| GPT-2 XL | 83.5 (79.6) | 85.4 (82.6) | 76.6 (69.5) |

**Classifiers.** Our primary classifier is a Random Forest (200 trees, 5-fold stratified CV); comparisons with CORAL (Cao et al., 2020), DwEye (Rasan and Chen, 2026), and other baselines in §5.

---

### 4 The Depth Degradation Atlas

The Depth Degradation Atlas maps how statistical fingerprints evolve across recursive generation depths, models, and decoding strategies: 3 × 3 = 9 model-strategy cells at depths d ∈ {0, 1, 2, 3}, with extensions to d=5 for EDD validation (§4.3).

#### 4.1 In-Distribution Performance

Table 2 reports four-class Random Forest accuracy (5-fold CV, 200 trees) across all nine cells. Accuracy ranges from 69.6% (Pythia, top-k) to 85.4% (GPT-2 XL, temperature), all exceeding the 25% chance baseline. GPT-2 XL achieves the highest accuracy under every strategy (76.6–85.4%), followed by OLMo (74.2–82.0%) and Pythia (69.6–78.2%). top-k yields the lowest in every model. The mean within-model strategy gap (4.4 pp) is comparable to the within-strategy model gap (7.1 pp)—decoding strategy and model family contribute roughly equally to performance variation.

Depth-0 recall exceeds 98% in all 9 cells; among generated depths, d2 consistently yields the lowest recall (46–73%), reflecting overlap with both adjacent classes (full per-class recall in Appendix A.3).

#### 4.2 Feature Consistency Across the Grid

Despite the 15.8 pp accuracy spread, a small feature family dominates universally. P90_PPL ranks top-2 by Gini importance in all 9 cells; VAR_SURPRISAL ranks in 8/9 under SHAP (79 Gini; full per-cell rankings in Table 16, Appendix A.15). Cross-model Spearman correlation averages ρ = 0.868; models agree on which features carry depth information. Feature ablation confirms concentration: top-2 features alone reach 91.1%

**A.9 Domain Bias Analysis**

To assess whether the classifiers exploit depth-related features or stylistic/topic cues from individual seed articles, we conduct three sub-experiments.

**Methodological note.** An initial implementation assigned sample IDs with a global counter across depths, inadvertently correlating seed-group identity with depth (LOGO accuracy 64.0%, seed-group prediction 20.8%). We discovered the issue during internal review, corrected to per-depth seed assignment ensuring each group contains equal samples per depth, and re-ran all sub-experiments. The results below use the corrected pipeline; the initial (buggy) numbers are reported for transparency.

**Sub-A: Standard CV.** Five-fold CV accuracy on 3-class (d1/d2/d3) classification ranges from 59% to 82% across the 9 atlas cells (top-2 ≥ 5× above the 33.1% chance level), confirming that depth signal is the dominant classification factor.

**Sub-B: LOGO evaluation.** We assign each passage to one of 10 seed-article groups (balanced: each group contains equal samples per depth) and perform leave-one-group-out (LOGO) evaluation. Mean accuracy is 72.1% (range 59.5–81.6%), matching standard CV (72.6%) within noise (before fix: standard CV (72.6%) within noise before fix: standard CV group confound). Per-fold standard deviations range from 0.4pp to 1.4pp, indicating that cross-group generalization is comparable, as in within-group classification (§4.3).

**Sub-C: Negative control.** We train two classifiers on identical features: one predicting depth, the other predicting seed-group identity (10-class, chance = 10%). Depth prediction accuracy averages 72%+; seed-group prediction averages 10.2%—indistinguishable from chance (before fix: 20.8%), inflated by the depth-group confound. The depth-to-seed group accuracy ratio is 7.1:1, confirming that feature representation encodes depth but not seed-article identity.

Taken together, these results show that seed-article grouping has no measurable effect on depth estimation after correcting the group assignment: LOGO accuracy equals standard CV, and seed-group prediction is at chance.

**A.13 Cross-Boundary Generalization**

The preceding experiments assume a single model family generates all recursive depths. In practice, recursive contamination may traverse model boundaries: arXiv text generated by model A is used to train model B, whose output trains model C. We probe whether the depth signal persists under two relaxations of the single-model assumption.

**Cross-model recursive chains.** We construct a heterogeneous chain: human text (d0) → Pythia-1.4B generates d1 → OLMo-1B finetuned on Pythia-d1 generates d2 → GPT-2 XL finetuned on OLMo-d2 generates d3. Each recursive step uses a different model family, eliminating the possibility that depth signal arises from a single model's idiosyncratic behavior. A 4-class Random Forest achieves 84.75% accuracy (95% CI 81.0, 88.25), with per-depth F1 scores of 0.98 (d0), 0.88 (d1), 0.76 (d2), and 0.76 (d3). Pairwise AUC remains high: d0-vs-d1 = 0.999 and d2-vs-d3 = 0.91. These results suggest that distributional artifacts of recursive generation persist across model boundaries—providing preliminary evidence that the depth signal is a property of the recursive process itself rather than of any individual generator.

**Cross-domain transfer.** All prior experiments use WikiText-103 as the seed corpus. To test domain dependence, we repeat the pipeline with arXiv abstracts as the seed text (Pythia-1.4B, nucleus p=0.95, 500 samples per depth, d0–d3). Five-fold cross-validation yields 74.1% ± 2.0% accuracy,

The 4pp accuracy gap relative to WikiText likely reflects the narrower stylistic range of scientific abstracts, which may reduce the distributional contrast between adjacent depths. These results suggest that the depth signal is domain-independent, providing preliminary evidence that the perplexity-based features capture properties of the recursive generation process rather than domain-specific artifacts of the seed corpus.

**A.14 Extended Discussion**

**Depth-graduated curation.** Current data curation operates on a binary human-vs-machine distinction (Xie et al., 2023; Weting et al., 2024). Recursive generation depth estimation enables a finer-grained alternative: retain low-depth generations (d1) whose distributional properties remain close to the human source, while down-weighting or filtering high-depth text (d3+) where tail erosion has degraded quality. The 70–85% in-distribution accuracy and EDD₃≥3 suggest depth-graduated filtering is feasible within known model–strategy configurations, though the d1/d2 boundary inversion under some strategy transfer (§5.3) means reliable curation requires either known decoding strategy metadata or an upstream strategy-identification step; a small-scale PoC (Appendix A.11) shows RF-filtered subsets match unfiltered quality with 44% of the data; large-scale validation remains open. Importance weighting (Sugiyama et al., 2007) could further enable continuous depth-aware data selection rather than discrete thresholding.

**Toward a provenance toolkit.** Depth estimation complements existing provenance methods along orthogonal axes. Watermarking (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023) provides high-confidence attribution when the generator cooperates but is inapplicable to unwatermarked text. Source attribution (Uchendu et al., 2020) identifies the generating model but not the generation history. Depth estimation characterizes *iterative reuse* regardless of generator cooperation or identity. A layered provenance system combining these three signals—watermark presence, source model, and recursive generation depth—could support more nuanced data auditing than any single method.

### 4.3 Monotonicity and EDD Analysis

Depth features exhibit strong monotonic trends: perplexity tail statistics decrease with depth (Spearman ρ = −1 across cell-level medians) while repetition features increase (trajectories in Figure 3, Appendix A.1). Inter-depth distances are monotonically uniform (d0-vs-d1 AUC exceeds 0.99 in all cells, whereas d2-vs-d3 ranges from 0.69 to 0.89.

We extend to depth d=5 for all three models under nucleus sampling, training dedicated binary RF classifiers (500 trees) for each adjacent pair (fig. 1). Figure 1 shows the AUC decay: Pythia-1.4B decays monotonically from 0.999 (d0|1) to 0.683 (d4|5), with the steepest drop between d0-2 and d2-3. The d3-vs-d4 AUC clusters near T=0.75 across all three models (0.750–0.784), while d4–d5 uniformly falls below 0.70, establishing a consistent depth-4 decay boundary. At T=0.75, 7/9 atlas cells maintain EDD ≥ 3 on the primary benchmark; at T=0.80, 3/9 (full threshold sensitivity in Table 17, Appendix A.16).

EDD uses binary-pair classifiers to avoid decision boundary dilution: in Pythia nucleus, d2-vs-d3 AUC degrades from 0.804 (4-class) to 0.689 (6-class) despite identical data.

### 4.4 Strategy-Dependent Trajectories

The three decoding strategies induce qualitatively distinct degradation trajectories. Nucleus (p=0.95) produces the most consistent accuracy (78.2–83.3%) and serves as the reference. Temperature (τ=0.9) yields the highest accuracy in 2/3 models because uniform logit scaling accelerates convergence to an attractor distribution (Shumailov et al., 2024), amplifying the fingerprint—but creating a boundary reversal risk where temperature depth 5 features approximate nucleus-only d-depth (N+1) features (§5). Top-1 (ε=50) produces the lowest accuracy (69.6–76.6%) because hard vocabulary truncation removes depth-discriminative low-probability tokens, though feature direction is preserved (cross-model ρ = 0.811). The strategy effect (8.4 pp range) exceeds the model effect (7.1 pp).

### 5 Generalization and Robustness

We evaluate generalization along seven axes: four below—classifier choice (§5.1), cross-model transfer (§5.2), cross-strategy transfer (§5.3), and cross-scale (§5.4)—and three in the Appendix (end-to-end learning, temperature robustness, cross-boundary transfer).

### 5.1 Baseline Comparison

Table 3 evaluates RF, XGBoost, and LightGBM on the same 19 features across three atlas cells. Per-cell spread is <0.4pp, establishing a feature-determined ceiling independent of the learning algorithm. CORAL ordinal regression (Cao et al., 2020) and DeBERTa (Bhasin and Chen, 2026) match RF within 0.1 pp (ρ > 0.05); all feature-based methods significantly outperform CE-MLP (74.9%) and logistic regression (75.0%). Single-feature regression on mean perplexity performs at chance (25.3 ± 1%); two zero-shot LLMs—DeepSeek-V3.2 (26.5%, 95% CI [22.0, 31.0]) and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (30.4%, [26.5, 34.6])—also fail, with an accuracy gap exceeding 42 pp vs. RF. Figure 2 shows all near-perfectly identified; errors concentrate at d2/d3.

### 5.2 Cross-Model Transfer

### 5.3 Cross-Strategy Transfer

We train on two decoding strategies and test on the held-out third (Table 5).

Mean cross-strategy accuracy (59.1%) falls 7pp below cross-model (66.4%). Training on nucleus + top-k and testing on temperature inverts the d1/d2 boundary (d1/2 AUC < 0.5); per-strategy z-score normalization partially recovers it but leaves a residual gap (4 limitations). A multi-temperature ablation (Appendix A.6) confirms within-τ robustness for τ ∈ [0.9 ±0.12] AUC < 0.00 but cross-τ transfer (mean 46.7%) is harder than cross-strategy transfer. End-to-end PLMs (DeBERTa-V3, RoBERTa) achieve only ~59%, lagging RF and >1pp, confirming depth signal resides in perplexity tail statistics inaccessible to standard PLM representations (Appendix A.8).

Both 7–8B models substantially exceed chance: Llama-3.1-8B at 70.2% and Qwen2.5-7B at 60.1%, with d0 separability preserved (AUC > 0.949). Llama-3.1-8B matches smaller models at EDD∈[3,4] with monotonic AUC decay; Qwen2.5-7B achieves EDD_0.70 = 5 via a non-monotonic (U-shaped) trajectory where AUC recovers after a d2-d3 minimum (consecutive AUC profiles in Table 18, Appendix A.17). Per-step signal strength decreases at larger scale (mean consecutive AUC 0.78 vs. 0.85 at 1–1.5B), and the divergent trajectories suggest instruction tuning may alter degradation dynamics, though further architectures are needed. Cross-model recursive chains (84.7%) and cross-domain transfer (arXiv 74.1%) further confirm signal universality (Appendix A.13).

### 6 Discussion and Conclusion

We formulated recursive generation depth estimation and showed that a compact feature set dominated by perplexity tail statistics achieves 70–85% four-class accuracy (EDD_0.75=4 across models), with five features sufficing for 97.6% of full performance and classifier-agnostic convergence within ≤0.4pp. The dominant pair (p90\_ppl, top-2 in 99 cells, var\_surprisal in 8/9 under SHAP) generalizes across the three studied model families without retraining, making depth estimation a candidate early-warning signal for model collapse (Shumailov et al., 2024). Recent work corrob-

(continuation of Section 6 — Discussion and Conclusion):

orates this connection, identifying entropy decline as a measurable signal of recursive degradation that parallels the tail erosion our features capture (Shi et al., 2025). Zero-shot LLM baselines (DeepSeek-V3.2, 26.5%; Qwen2.5-7B, 30.4%) perform near chance, confirming that depth discrimination requires computed statistical features rather than general language understanding.

Cross-strategy transfer remains the primary bottleneck (59.1% vs. 66.4% cross-model), with the temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion making single-classifier deployment across unknown strategies infeasible; strategy-conditioned classifiers—preceded by automatic strategy identification exploiting distinguishable perplexity signatures—offer a practical path, particularly since single-platform deployment typically knows the decoding strategy a priori.

Depth estimation enables graduated data curation beyond the binary human/machine distinction (Xie et al., 2025; Wrtg et al., 2024): a proof-of-concept shows RF-filtered subsets match unfiltered quality with 44% of the data (Appendix A.11). As a provenance signal, it complements watermarking (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023) and source attribution (Chenela et al., 2020) by characterizing iterative reuse regardless of generator identity (Revirsdorff et al., 2025). Cross-scale experiments (§5.4) confirm signal persistence at 7–8B scale with divergent AUC trajectories across architectures, suggesting instruction tuning may alter degradation dynamics; extending to segment-level estimation introduces a granularity–statistical-power tradeoff.

**Limitations**

**Cross-strategy deployment constraint.** Cross-strategy transfer induces a d1/d2 boundary inversion under temperature sampling. Per-strategy z-score normalization partially corrects the inver-

sion under logistic regression (GPT-2 XL, d1/v2 AUC 0.24→0.56, OLMo 0.19→0.71) but yields negligible improvement for the Random Forest classifier used throughout the main experiments (Δ < 0.02 pp), and even in the best case (logistic regression) leaves a residual gap relative to within-strategy performance (ε>0.50), indicating that a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification → strategy-conditioned classification) is needed for reliable cross-strategy deployment.

**d0 inflation of headline metrics.** Depth 0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall >98%) across all nine model-strategy settings, inflating headline accuracy. Cross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).

**Controlled vs. ecological setting.** The primary benchmark uses Wikipedia seed text with controlled recursive generators (LoRA fine-tuned, 1–1.5B parameter models); cross-scale experiments extend to 7–8B instruction-tuned models (§5.4). This protocol isolates the recursive depth variable but diverges from wild recursive contamination, where models are pretrained on mixed corpora containing post-generation outputs as unknown proportions; the fingerprints we identify may attenuate or shift under such diffuse exposure. Depth signal is the dominant classification factor (5-fold CV 95-82%), up to 2.5× chance. LOGO accuracy (72.1%) matches standard CV (72.0%), and subgroup prediction is at chance (10.25 vs. 10%; Appendix A.9). The 7–8B experiments use instruction-tuned models: only; whether base models at this scale exhibit the same signal profile remains open. Real-world documents may also interleave segments at different recursive generation depths, extending to segment-level estimation introduces a granularity–statistical-power tradeoff.

**Domain-dependent false positive rate.** On editorial text (WikiText-103), all classifiers achieve >98.5% d0 accuracy, but on web-crawl data (C4, 5,000 passages), FPR ranges from 4.7% (OLMo) to 22.4% (GPT-2 XL). Mislassification concentrates in template/SEO content with elevated repetition features (rep\_3gram +37%, rep\_4gram +75% vs. correctly classified d0); the model gap likely reflects training data composition (OLMo's Dolma includes diverse web data vs. Pythia/ GPT-2 XL's Wikipedia/WebText). Deployment on

---

## PAGE 8 (main_p8.png)

(continuation of Limitations):

heterogeneous web corpora requires model- and domain-specific calibration.

**Adversarial robustness.** Adversarial paraphrasing (Sadasivan et al., 2023) could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.

**EDD monotonicity assumption.** Our EDD definition (Eq. 1) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth d* to exceed T, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically—as observed in all our configurations. However, Bakshi and Chakraborty (2026) show that early recursion can temporarily improve model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d3/d5). Our cross-strategy results provide an empirical example of non-monotonic: training on nucleus + top-k and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2 XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption. In such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work. The choice of threshold T is also application-dependent: at T=0.80, several cells lose one depth level relative to T=0.75.

**Reference model dependency.** Surprisal-based features are computed relative to Pythia-1.4B, which coincides with one of the three generators. For the Pythia pipeline this constitutes self-model feature extraction, while OLMo and GPT-2 XL measurements are cross-model. Empirically, the self-model configuration does not yield the highest accuracy (Pythia 78.2% vs. GPT-2 XL 85.4%), suggesting the overlap does not confer a systematic advantage. An ablation with OLMo-1B as reference model shows 2-4pp (±2.3), suggesting moderate robustness; however, both reference models share similar scale (~1B) and autoregressive architecture, so validation with architecturally distinct references (e.g., encoder-only or larger-scale models) remains open. The choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.

**Additional caveats.** Detection features degrade under domain shift (Pudasaini et al., 2026); our depth features are likely susceptible. Falashi et al. (2026) show that curated synthetic data need not trigger collapse, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.

### Ethics Statement

This work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2 XL) and Wikipedia text as seed. No human subjects were involved, no private or sensitive data were collected, and no new models were released. Our method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research. Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

Cross-scale uses Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct under 4-bit NF4 QLoRA.

**Limitations section:** Six explicit limitations — cross-strategy deployment constraint, d0 inflation of headline metrics, controlled vs. ecological setting gap, domain-dependent FPR, adversarial robustness (untested), EDD monotonicity assumption, reference model dependency, and additional caveats about domain shift and curated synthetic data.

A multi-temperature ablation (Appendix A.6) confirms within-τ robustness for τ ∈ [0.9 ±0.12] AUC < 0.00 but cross-τ transfer (mean 46.7%) is harder than cross-strategy transfer. End-to-end PLMs (DeBERTa-V3, RoBERTa) achieve only ~59%, lagging RF and >1pp, confirming depth signal resides in perplexity tail statistics inaccessible to standard PLM representations (Appendix A.8).\n\n### 5.4 Cross-Scale Analysis\n\nWe extend to four 7–8B models—Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Team, 2025) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024)—under 4-bit NF4 QLoRA, generating depths d ∈ {0,...,5} with nucleus sampling (500 samples/depth). Cross-model recursive chains (84.7%) and cross-domain transfer (arXiv 74.1%) further confirm signal universality (Appendix A.13).\n\n### 6 Discussion and Conclusion\n\nWe formulated recursive generation depth estimation and showed that a compact feature set dominated by perplexity tail statistics achieves 70–85% four-class accuracy (EDD_0.75=4 across models), with five features sufficing for 97.6% of full performance and classifier-agnostic convergence within ≤0.4pp. The dominant pair (p90\\_ppl, top-2 in 99 cells, var\\_surprisal in 8/9 under SHAP) generalizes across the three studied model families without retraining, making depth estimation a candidate early-warning signal for model collapse (Shumailov et al., 2024). Zero-shot LLM baselines (DeepSeek-V3.2, 26.5%; Qwen2.5-7B, 30.4%) perform near chance, confirming that depth discrimination requires computed statistical features rather than general language understanding.\n\nCross-strategy transfer remains the primary bottleneck (59.1% vs. 66.4% cross-model), with the temperature-induced d1/d2 AUC inversion making single-classifier deployment across unknown strategies infeasible; strategy-conditioned classifiers—preceded by automatic strategy identification exploiting distinguishable perplexity signatures—offer a practical path, particularly since single-platform deployment typically knows the decoding strategy a priori.\n\nDepth estimation enables graduated data curation beyond the binary human/machine distinction (Xie et al., 2025; Wrtg et al., 2024): a proof-of-concept shows RF-filtered subsets match unfiltered quality with 44% of the data (Appendix A.11). As a provenance signal, it complements watermarking (Kirchenbauer et al., 2023) and source attribution (Chenela et al., 2020) by characterizing iterative reuse regardless of generator identity (Revirsdorff et al., 2025). Cross-scale experiments (§5.4) confirm signal persistence at 7–8B scale with divergent AUC trajectories across architectures, suggesting instruction tuning may alter degradation dynamics; extending to segment-level estimation introduces a granularity–statistical-power tradeoff.\n\n**Limitations**\n\n**Cross-strategy deployment constraint.** Cross-strategy transfer induces a d1/d2 boundary inversion under temperature sampling. Per-strategy z-score normalization partially corrects the inver-\n\nsion under logistic regression (GPT-2 XL, d1/v2 AUC 0.24→0.56, OLMo 0.19→0.71) but yields negligible improvement for the Random Forest classifier used throughout the main experiments (Δ < 0.02 pp), and even in the best case (logistic regression) leaves a residual gap relative to within-strategy performance (ε>0.50), indicating that a two-stage pipeline (strategy identification → strategy-conditioned classification) is needed for reliable cross-strategy deployment.\n\n**d0 inflation of headline metrics.** Depth 0 (human-written text) is near-perfectly separable (recall >98%) across all nine model-strategy settings, inflating headline accuracy. Cross-model transfer accuracy of 66.4% is substantially driven by d0; d2 recall drops to 26.8% in the worst case (Pythia holdout).\n\n**Controlled vs. ecological setting.** The primary benchmark uses Wikipedia seed text with controlled recursive generators (LoRA fine-tuned, 1–1.5B parameter models); cross-scale experiments extend to 7–8B instruction-tuned models (§5.4). This protocol isolates the recursive depth variable but diverges from wild recursive contamination, where models are pretrained on mixed corpora containing post-generation outputs as unknown proportions; the fingerprints we identify may attenuate or shift under such diffuse exposure. Depth signal is the dominant classification factor (5-fold CV 95-82%), up to 2.5× chance. LOGO accuracy (72.1%) matches standard CV (72.0%), and subgroup prediction is at chance (10.25 vs. 10%; Appendix A.9). The 7–8B experiments use instruction-tuned models: only; whether base models at this scale exhibit the same signal profile remains open. Real-world documents may also interleave segments at different recursive generation depths, extending to segment-level estimation introduces a granularity–statistical-power tradeoff.\n\n**Domain-dependent false positive rate.** On editorial text (WikiText-103), all classifiers achieve >98.5% d0 accuracy, but on web-crawl data (C4, 5,000 passages), FPR ranges from 4.7% (OLMo) to 22.4% (GPT-2 XL). Mislassification concentrates in template/SEO content with elevated repetition features (rep\\_3gram +37%, rep\\_4gram +75% vs. correctly classified d0); the model gap likely reflects training data composition (OLMo's Dolma includes diverse web data vs. Pythia/ GPT-2 XL's Wikipedia/WebText). Deployment on\n\n---\n\n## PAGE 8 (main_p8.png)\n\n(continuation of Limitations):\n\nheterogeneous web corpora requires model- and domain-specific calibration.\n\n**Adversarial robustness.** Adversarial paraphrasing (Sadasivan et al., 2023) could disrupt the perplexity tail features that drive classification; depth estimation's robustness under such attacks is untested.\n\n**EDD monotonicity assumption.** Our EDD definition (Eq. 1) requires all pairwise AUCs up to depth d* to exceed T, which is well-behaved when AUC decays monotonically—as observed in all our configurations. However, Bakshi and Chakraborty (2026) show that early recursion can temporarily improve model quality, which could produce non-monotonic AUC profiles (e.g., a dip at d1/d2 followed by recovery at d3/d5). Our cross-strategy results provide an empirical example of non-monotonic: training on nucleus + top-k and testing on temperature yields d1-vs-d2 AUC as low as 0.129 (GPT-2 XL) and 0.253 (OLMo), violating the monotonicity assumption. In such cases EDD would conservatively report a lower value than the deepest discriminable pair, potentially underestimating the true discriminable range; extending EDD to handle non-contiguous discriminable regions is future work. The choice of threshold T is also application-dependent: at T=0.80, several cells lose one depth level relative to T=0.75.\n\n**Reference model dependency.** Surprisal-based features are computed relative to Pythia-1.4B, which coincides with one of the three generators. For the Pythia pipeline this constitutes self-model feature extraction, while OLMo and GPT-2 XL measurements are cross-model. Empirically, the self-model configuration does not yield the highest accuracy (Pythia 78.2% vs. GPT-2 XL 85.4%), suggesting the overlap does not confer a systematic advantage. An ablation with OLMo-1B as reference model shows 2-4pp (±2.3), suggesting moderate robustness; however, both reference models share similar scale (~1B) and autoregressive architecture, so validation with architecturally distinct references (e.g., encoder-only or larger-scale models) remains open. The choice of reference model affects feature values; a different reference model may shift absolute feature magnitudes and potentially alter discriminability at depth boundaries.\n\n**Additional caveats.** Detection features degrade under domain shift (Pudasaini et al., 2026); our depth features are likely susceptible. Falashi et al. (2026) show that curated synthetic data need not trigger collapse, attenuating the fingerprints we exploit.\n\n### Ethics Statement\n\nThis work uses publicly available pretrained language models (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, GPT-2 XL) and Wikipedia text as seed. Our method is intended to support data provenance and training-data auditing; we acknowledge that depth estimation tools could in principle be misused to circumvent content moderation, though such risks are shared with all detection-oriented research.
